params.question: A forensic science laboratory analyst classifies a poison by its origin, while the treating emergency physician classifies the same poison by its mechanism of action. Which of the following best explains why this dual classification framework exists in toxicology?

answers.text: The origin classification is used only in court proceedings, while the action classification is used only for academic teaching

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Both classifications have direct practical applications. Origin guides laboratory analysis; action guides clinical management. Neither is limited to courts or classrooms.

answers.text: Classification by origin guides the forensic laboratory's choice of analytical method, while classification by action guides the clinician's choice of treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. For example, knowing a poison is synthetic (origin) tells the FSL to use methods suited to organophosphates, while knowing it is neurotic (action) tells the clinician to anticipate nervous system effects and choose the appropriate antidote.

answers.text: Action classification is more scientifically accurate and has replaced the older origin classification in modern practice

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Neither classification is outdated. Both remain essential — one serves the forensic analyst and the other serves the treating physician.

answers.text: Both classifications serve the same clinical purpose but use different terminology depending on the region of India

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The two frameworks serve fundamentally different users with different needs — the forensic laboratory and the treating clinician, respectively.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: classification by origin (animal, vegetable, mineral, synthetic) tells the forensic lab which analytical technique to apply, while classification by action (corrosive, irritant, neurotic, cardiac, asphyxiant) tells the clinician which organs are at risk and what treatment to use.

Well done! The dual framework exists because forensic analysts need to know the chemical source to choose the right extraction and detection method, while clinicians need to know the mechanism of harm to anticipate organ damage and select the correct antidote.

params.question: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after ingesting several iron tablets in a suicide attempt. The intern plans to administer activated charcoal. Why should this plan be reconsidered?

answers.text: The ingestion occurred more than 30 minutes ago, so charcoal is no longer effective for any substance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Activated charcoal is most effective within the first hour of ingestion, so 45 minutes is still within the therapeutic window for susceptible substances. The time alone does not rule it out.

answers.text: Activated charcoal is contraindicated in all deliberate self-harm cases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. There is no blanket contraindication to charcoal in self-harm. The decision depends on the substance ingested and the time since ingestion, not the intent.

answers.text: Iron is not adsorbed by activated charcoal, so it would provide no benefit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Iron, along with lithium and alcohols, is not adsorbed by activated charcoal. Administering it here would offer no therapeutic benefit and could cause complications such as aspiration or obscured endoscopic visualisation.

answers.text: Iron tablets are too large in physical size to be bound by charcoal particles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The limitation is chemical, not physical. Iron ions are simply not adsorbed onto the charcoal surface, regardless of tablet size.

overallFeedback.feedback: Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron, lithium, or alcohols. These exceptions must be remembered, as giving charcoal for these substances provides no benefit. Alternative decontamination strategies must be considered.

Correct! Iron is one of several substances that activated charcoal cannot adsorb. Knowing these exceptions — iron, lithium, and alcohols — is critical to avoid giving ineffective treatment and to pursue appropriate alternatives.

interactions.label: An unconscious patient is brought to the emergency department with suspected poi

params.question: An unconscious patient is brought to the emergency department with suspected poisoning. The pulse oximeter reads 98%, yet the patient appears clinically cyanotic. Based on bedside assessment principles, which poisoning most likely explains this discrepancy?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Organophosphate poisoning produces a cholinergic toxidrome (pinpoint pupils, excessive secretions) but does not cause a falsely normal pulse oximetry reading.

Correct. Standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so they display a falsely normal saturation even when significant CO poisoning is present. Co-oximetry is essential in suspected carbon monoxide exposure.
Incorrect. Paracetamol toxicity causes hepatic damage over hours to days but does not interfere with pulse oximetry readings or produce this clinical discrepancy.
Incorrect. Salicylate poisoning causes metabolic disturbances and tachypnoea but does not produce a falsely normal pulse oximetry reading in a cyanotic patient.

overallFeedback.feedback: Carbon monoxide poisoning is the classic cause of falsely normal pulse oximetry. The device cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. Always request co-oximetry in suspected CO exposure.

Correct! Pulse oximetry gives falsely reassuring readings in carbon monoxide poisoning because the device mistakes carboxyhaemoglobin for oxyhaemoglobin. Always order co-oximetry when CO exposure is suspected — relying on SpO₂ alone can be fatal.

params.question: In a medico-legal autopsy, white soapy-looking burns around the mouth and oesophagus indicate ingestion of a strong acid.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. White, soapy-looking burns are characteristic of alkali ingestion (liquefactive necrosis and saponification), not acid. Strong acids cause coagulative necrosis, producing grey or black tissue damage. Confusing the two can misdirect the entire forensic investigation.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. White, soapy-looking burns result from alkali ingestion, which causes liquefactive necrosis and saponification of tissue fats. Strong acids, in contrast, cause coagulative necrosis producing grey or black tissue damage. This distinction is critical during the external examination to guide the forensic science laboratory toward the correct substance.

interactions.label: The video describes methylmercury in water and organochlorine pesticides like DD

params.question: The video describes methylmercury in water and organochlorine pesticides like DDT in soil as particularly dangerous environmental toxins. What shared property makes both disproportionately harmful to humans at the top of the food chain?

answers.text: Both are highly volatile and spread rapidly through the air, causing widespread acute inhalation injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Neither methylmercury nor DDT spreads primarily through air. Their danger lies in their persistence in water and soil and their progressive accumulation through biological food chains.

answers.text: Both cause acute poisoning symptoms within hours of even minimal exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Both substances typically cause chronic, low-dose effects rather than acute poisoning. Their danger is cumulative — building up over months to years of dietary exposure.

answers.text: Both are exclusively absorbed through the skin, bypassing hepatic first-pass metabolism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. These substances enter the body primarily through ingestion of contaminated food. Their danger is not route-specific but lies in their environmental persistence and biological accumulation.

answers.text: Both persist in the environment and undergo biomagnification, reaching their highest concentrations in top predators

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Both methylmercury and organochlorines resist degradation, persist for years to decades, and biomagnify — each trophic level accumulates higher concentrations than the one below. This is exactly the mechanism behind Minamata disease, where humans consuming contaminated fish suffered devastating neurological damage.

overallFeedback.feedback: The shared property is persistence and biomagnification. Both methylmercury and DDT resist breakdown, remain in the environment for years, and concentrate progressively up the food chain — so humans, as top predators, receive disproportionately high doses.

Well done! Persistence and biomagnification are the common thread. These substances concentrate at each trophic level, so top predators including humans accumulate body burdens far exceeding environmental concentrations — the pattern the video identified across all three media of pollution.
